title: Crescent shawl in treble
subtitle: A curved crescent shape worked in rows of treble with short-row shaping at each edge
excerpt: A crescent shawl sits close to the neck and drapes across the shoulders in a gentle curve. This version is worked in treble on a 4 mm hook with DK yarn, using simple edge increases to build the crescent shape over roughly 40 rows. Finished width is about 160 cm along the curved lower edge; depth is about 35 cm at the centre point.
sourceNotes: Crescent shaping technique synthesised from Weldon's Practical Crochet Volume 3 (1887), which describes increasing at the selvedge of rectangular shawls to create curved lower edges (Internet Archive). General treble-stitch construction from de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886).

glossaryTerms.definition: A shawl construction that increases stitches at both ends of every row and at evenly spaced points across the row, building a curved lower edge that sits away from the body.

content.text: A crescent shawl hugs the neck and fans across both shoulders in a curved arc. This pattern works in rows of treble (UK tr, the same move US patterns call double crochet) on a 4 mm hook, with increases at both ends of every row plus three increase points across the centre of alternate rows. The result of this
crescent shaping
is a curved lower edge about 160 cm wide.

attrs.title: Materials
attrs.body: Approximately 350 g DK-weight yarn, merino or merino-blend is warm and holds the block well. A 4 mm hook (US G/6). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers (3). Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.

content.text: Gauge

18 tr × 10 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK yarn with a 4 mm hook, measured unstretched. Swatch before beginning and adjust hook size if needed: one stitch per 10 cm off changes the finished width by about 9 cm at the final row count.
Stitches used
chain (ch): UK and US shared.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
Pattern

The shawl is worked flat, turning at the end of each row. On increase rows (rows 2, 4, 6 etc.) three internal increase points sit at roughly one-quarter, one-half, and three-quarters of the row width. Mark these with stitch markers and move them up on each row.
Foundation chain
Ch 41. (This is the starting top edge, measuring approximately 22 cm.)
Row 1 (right side)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in each ch across. Turn. (40 tr)
Row 2 (increase row)

Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 2 tr in the first st (edge increase). 1 tr in each of next 8 sts. Place marker. 2 tr in the next st (centre-left increase). 1 tr in each of next 18 sts. Place marker. 2 tr in the next st (centre increase). 1 tr in each of next 8 sts. Place marker. 2 tr in the next st (centre-right increase). 1 tr in the last st. 2 tr in the last st (edge increase). Turn. (46 tr)
Row 3 (plain row)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in each st across. Turn. (46 tr)
Rows 4 to 40

Continue alternating increase rows (row 2 pattern, working the increases at the same marked positions plus at both ends) and plain rows (row 3 pattern). On each increase row, work 2 tr at the beginning, 2 tr at each of the three internal markers (moving markers after each increase row), and 2 tr at the end. By row 40 you have approximately 160 sts.

attrs.title: Keeping the crescent curve
attrs.body: The three internal increase points must stay evenly spaced as the row count grows. On every increase row, the middle marker should sit at the centre of the row count; if it drifts more than 2 stitches from centre, move it back before working the increase.

content.text: Finishing

Fasten off and weave in all ends. Wet-block by soaking in cool water for 10 minutes, pressing water out gently, then pinning to shape on a blocking mat. Pin the two top corners first to hold the straight upper edge, then pin the curved lower edge at 10 cm intervals, easing the crescent shape gently.
Care
Handwash in cool water with mild wool wash. Lay flat to dry. Do not tumble-dry or hang. Wet treble fabric will stretch under its own weight.
What to try next

Work the same crescent construction in a shell stitch pattern on every row instead of plain treble for a lighter, more open fabric. A lace-weight single crochet version on a 2.5 mm hook makes a finer shawlette suitable for summer wear.
